title: 8  Tactical Financial Analysis
text:
8.1 Introduction
Strategic asset allocation, the subject of Chapter 7, establishes the long-term policy mix. It anchors the portfolio. It determines exposure to systematic risk factors and drives the bulk of long-term returns. But the policy mix is static by design. It does not respond to changing market conditions, shifting valuations, or emerging opportunities.
Tactical asset allocation fills this gap. It is the deliberate, short-term deviation from the strategic allocation, designed to capitalize on perceived market mispricing or macroeconomic shifts. If the strategic allocation calls for 50 percent equities, a tactical overlay might increase that to 55 percent when equities appear cheap relative to bonds, or reduce it to 45 percent when they appear expensive. These deviations are temporary. They are reversed when the mispricing corrects or the opportunity passes.
A fundamental distinction separates the two approaches. Strategic allocation provides the beta—the market return that comes from broad, sustained exposure to asset classes. Tactical allocation seeks alpha—the excess return that comes from timing those exposures successfully. Beta is earned by staying invested. Alpha is earned by being right about short-term market movements. One is a matter of discipline. The other is a bet on foresight.
Alpha is seductive. The promise of outperformance attracts capital and talent, fueling an industry of strategists, forecasters, and active managers. Yet tactical asset allocation operates in a zero-sum environment. For every investor who beats the market through well-timed trades, another investor loses. The gains of the successful timer are the losses of the unsuccessful one. Arithmetic leaves no room for ambiguity. The average investor earns the market return, less costs. Tactical allocation adds layers of cost: transaction fees, bid-ask spreads, and, in taxable accounts, capital gains taxes. To succeed, the tactical allocator must not only be right about market direction but right by enough to overcome these frictions.
The evidence is sobering. Decades of research on mutual fund performance demonstrate that most active managers underperform their benchmarks after fees. Market timing proves difficult to sustain. Short-term movements are driven by news, sentiment, and capital flows—forces that resist consistent prediction. Even skilled investors with disciplined processes struggle to add value through tactical adjustments over extended periods.
This does not render tactical allocation futile. It demands humility. Deviations from the strategic allocation should be modest, grounded in a clear and testable thesis, and evaluated over periods long enough to separate skill from luck. A sound process will endure stretches of underperformance. That is the nature of the endeavor. What matters is whether the process adds value over a full cycle, net of costs.
We turn now to the tools and frameworks that support tactical financial analysis. The sources of tactical opportunity will be examined. Methods for evaluating those opportunities will be explored. The disciplines required for effective implementation will be set out. Valuation signals, momentum, sentiment indicators, and macroeconomic analysis each play a role. So too do the behavioral pitfalls that make tactical allocation harder in practice than it appears on paper. The aim is not to promise easy alpha. It is to provide a clear-eyed assessment of what tactical allocation can achieve—and what it cannot.

title: 8  Tactical Financial Analysis
section: 8.2 Theoretical Foundation: Why TAA is Possible (and Hard)
text:
8.2 Theoretical Foundation: Why TAA is Possible (and Hard)
Before examining how tactical asset allocation is implemented, we must understand why it might work—and why it so often fails. The theoretical foundation rests on three pillars: the Efficient Market Hypothesis, the behavioral critique of that hypothesis, and the Fundamental Law of Active Management, which quantifies the conditions under which tactical deviations can add value.
The Efficient Market Hypothesis, or EMH, provides the baseline. Markets are efficient when prices fully reflect all available information. Three forms of efficiency are commonly distinguished. Weak-form efficiency holds that past prices and trading volumes cannot be used to predict future prices. Technical analysis, which relies on patterns in historical data, should not generate excess returns in a weak-form efficient market. Semi-strong form efficiency goes further, asserting that all publicly available information is already embedded in prices. Neither fundamental analysis nor the study of earnings reports, economic data, or news releases can reliably produce alpha. Strong-form efficiency, the most restrictive version, holds that even private information is reflected in prices, leaving no room for any investor to earn excess returns consistently.
Under strong-form efficiency, tactical asset allocation is futile. No amount of analysis or insight can beat the market because the market already knows everything worth knowing. Under semi-strong or weak-form efficiency, some scope for tactical deviations may exist, but it is narrow. The investor must possess information or analytical capabilities not yet reflected in prices.
Markets, however, are not perfectly efficient. Decades of research in behavioral finance have documented systematic departures from rationality. Investors overreact to recent news and underreact to longer-term trends. They chase performance, buying assets that have already appreciated and selling those that have declined. Fear and greed drive prices away from fair value, creating pockets of mispricing. These behavioral wedges open the door for tactical allocation. When sentiment pushes an asset class to an extreme, a disciplined tactical investor can take the other side of the trade, selling when others are greedy and buying when they are fearful.
The challenge lies in timing. Behavioral mispricing can persist for longer than a rational investor expects. A tactical position taken too early is indistinguishable from a wrong one. The market can remain irrational longer than the tactical allocator can remain solvent, as the saying goes. The behavioral critique explains why opportunities exist. It does not guarantee that they can be exploited.
Richard Grinold’s Fundamental Law of Active Management provides the framework for evaluating whether a tactical process can succeed. The law states that the information ratio, a measure of risk-adjusted excess return, depends on two factors: skill and breadth.
\[
IR = IC \times \sqrt{BR}
\]
The Information Ratio, or IR, captures the quality of the tactical process. It is the excess return generated per unit of active risk taken. A higher IR indicates a more efficient conversion of risk into return.
The Information Coefficient, or IC, measures skill. It is the correlation between the forecaster’s predictions and the actual outcomes. An IC of 1.0 indicates perfect foresight. An IC of 0.0 indicates no predictive ability whatsoever. In practice, ICs in financial markets are modest. A correlation of 0.10 between forecasts and realizations is considered strong. Most tactical processes operate with ICs far lower.
Breadth, or BR, counts the number of independent bets placed over the evaluation period. A tactical process that makes one large allocation decision per year has low breadth. A process that evaluates multiple asset classes, regions, and factors on a quarterly basis has higher breadth. Breadth is the multiplier. It amplifies the impact of skill.
The square root relationship is important. Doubling breadth does not double the information ratio. It increases it by a factor of roughly 1.4. The implication is clear. To achieve a meaningful information ratio, a tactical process needs either exceptional skill or substantial breadth. In practice, both are scarce.
Consider a tactical allocator with an IC of 0.10, a reasonable estimate for a disciplined process. If this allocator makes four independent bets per year, the information ratio is 0.10 times the square root of four, or 0.20. An IR of 0.20 is modest. Over time, it would generate a small but positive excess return. Increasing breadth to sixteen independent bets per year would raise the IR to 0.40, a more meaningful level. But finding sixteen genuinely independent tactical opportunities is difficult. Asset class returns are correlated. Economic events affect multiple markets simultaneously. The assumption of independence is often violated.
The Fundamental Law clarifies why tactical asset allocation is hard. Skill, as measured by the IC, is bounded. No forecaster is consistently prescient. Breadth is constrained. The number of independent opportunities available in any year is limited. The product of these two factors, even under favorable assumptions, produces information ratios that are modest. When costs are subtracted—transaction fees, taxes, and the expenses of research and implementation—the net alpha available to the tactical allocator shrinks further.
This does not mean tactical allocation should be abandoned. It means expectations must be calibrated. A tactical process with a realistic IC and adequate breadth can add value over time. But the value added will be small, measured in tens of basis points rather than percentage points of excess return. The process will experience extended drawdowns. It will test the conviction of those who implement it.
The theoretical foundation yields a practical conclusion. Tactical deviations should be modest. The strategic allocation does the heavy lifting. Tactical overlays provide a marginal contribution, one that is welcome but not essential. Framed this way, tactical asset allocation becomes a reasonable pursuit rather than a false promise. It is a search for incremental alpha, pursued with discipline and humility, grounded in a clear understanding of the odds.

title: 8  Tactical Financial Analysis
text:
8.3 Macro-Fundamental Tactical Analysis
Chapter 6 established the economic variables that drive long-term asset class returns. Tactical analysis uses those same variables differently. Rather than forming ten-year expectations, it focuses on momentum and surprises—the deviation of current data from consensus forecasts and the speed at which conditions are changing.
Economic surprise indices track how reported data compare to analyst expectations. When GDP growth, inflation, employment, or industrial production come in above consensus, the surprise is positive. When they fall short, it is negative. These surprises move markets. An economy that consistently beats expectations tends to see equity outperformance and bond underperformance, as growth strengthens and rate expectations adjust upward. An economy that consistently disappoints sees the opposite.
The tactical signal lies not in the level of the data but in its direction and momentum. A single positive surprise may be noise. A series of positive surprises suggests that the consensus is behind the curve, that conditions are improving faster than analysts recognize. The tactical allocator can position for further positive surprises by overweighting equities and underweighting bonds. The trade works until the consensus catches up, at which point the edge disappears.
Valuation spreads provide a different lens. Rather than asking whether an asset class is cheap in absolute terms, they ask whether it is cheap relative to another. The price-to-earnings ratio of US equities might be 20, while European equities trade at 14. This spread is wider than its historical average. The tactical question is whether it will narrow, and if so, in which direction.
Relative value trades rest on the assumption of mean reversion. Spreads that have widened beyond their historical range are expected to narrow. Spreads that have narrowed beyond their range are expected to widen. The tactical allocator overweights the cheap asset and underweights the dear one, betting on convergence.
The risk is that the spread reflects a structural shift rather than a temporary dislocation. US equities might deserve a permanently higher multiple because of a different sector composition, stronger earnings growth, or a lower cost of capital. If the world has changed, the historical range is no longer a reliable anchor. The tactical position loses money as the spread continues to widen rather than narrow.
The earnings yield gap, sometimes called the Fed Model, provides a framework for tactical allocation between equities and bonds. It compares the earnings yield of stocks—the inverse of the price-to-earnings ratio—to the yield on bonds.
\[
\text{Yield Gap} = \frac{E}{P} - Y_{\text{bond}}
\]
Where \(\frac{E}{P}\) is the earnings yield of the equity market and \(Y_{\text{bond}}\) is the yield on a reference bond, typically the ten-year government bond. A positive gap indicates that equities offer a higher earnings yield than bonds, making them relatively attractive. A negative gap indicates that bonds offer higher yields, making them relatively attractive.
The tactical signal is straightforward. When the yield gap is wide, equities are cheap relative to bonds. The tactical allocator overweights equities. When the gap is narrow or negative, bonds are cheap relative to equities. The tactical allocator overweights bonds.
History provides some support for this approach. Periods of wide yield gaps have often been followed by equity outperformance. Periods of narrow or negative gaps have often been followed by bond outperformance. The relationship is not mechanical. The yield gap was negative throughout much of the 1990s, yet equities delivered exceptional returns as earnings grew and valuations expanded. The signal can be early. It can be wrong for extended periods.
The tactical allocator must distinguish between a signal that is early and a signal that is broken. This requires judgment. The yield gap might narrow because bond yields are rising, which is typically negative for equities. Or it might narrow because earnings are growing, which is positive. The same metric can tell different stories depending on the underlying drivers.
Macro-fundamental tactical analysis integrates these approaches. Economic surprise indices provide information about the near-term trajectory of growth and inflation. Valuation spreads identify relative value opportunities across markets. The earnings yield gap frames the choice between equities and bonds. Each signal is imperfect on its own. Combined, they provide a more complete picture.
Yet the fundamental challenge remains. These signals are widely followed. Any edge they provide erodes as more investors act on them. The tactical allocator must be faster, more disciplined, or more insightful than the competition. That is a demanding standard. It is also the reason tactical deviations should remain modest, a complement to the strategic allocation rather than a replacement for it.

title: 8  Tactical Financial Analysis
text:
8.4 Sentiment and Behavioral Indicators
Macro-fundamental analysis examines economic data and valuation relationships. Sentiment analysis examines the mood of the market. When fear or greed reaches an extreme, prices disconnect from fundamentals. The tactical allocator who can identify these extremes can position for the reversal.
Sentiment indicators measure prevailing emotion. Some are derived from market prices, others from surveys, still others from the behavior of specific groups of market participants. The put-call ratio, for instance, measures the volume of put options traded relative to call options. Puts protect against declines. Calls provide exposure to gains. When the ratio is high, fear dominates and investors are paying up for protection. When the ratio is low, greed dominates and investors are chasing upside. Extreme readings in either direction suggest the market may be near a turning point, though the signal is noisy and requires confirmation from other sources.
The VIX, often called the fear index, measures the implied volatility of equity index options. It reflects the market’s expectation of future turbulence. A high VIX indicates that investors are willing to pay elevated premiums for protection. Historically, very high readings have coincided with market bottoms—the panic that drives the VIX higher also drives prices lower, creating the conditions for a rebound. A low VIX tells the opposite story. Very low readings suggest complacency, an underestimation of the potential for adverse moves. These periods of tranquility have sometimes preceded sharp corrections. Yet the VIX is not a precise timing tool. It can remain elevated for weeks during a prolonged selloff, or stay low for months while a bull market continues to climb.
Survey-based indicators capture sentiment more directly. The AAII Investor Sentiment Survey asks individual investors whether they are bullish, bearish, or neutral. When bullish sentiment reaches extreme levels, optimism is widespread. Most of the money that will flow into the market has already done so. The marginal buyer is exhausted. When bearish sentiment reaches extreme levels, pessimism is pervasive. Most of the selling has already occurred. The marginal seller is exhausted.
These indicators share a contrarian logic. They work best when they contradict the prevailing trend. A market making new highs accompanied by extreme bullish sentiment is vulnerable—the good news is already reflected in both prices and psychology. A market making new lows accompanied by extreme bearish sentiment may be nearing a bottom—the bad news is already discounted. The tactical allocator looks for these dislocations.
Herding behavior amplifies the dynamic. Investors take comfort in consensus. When prices rise, the sight of others profiting creates pressure to join. Momentum builds on itself. More buyers enter, prices rise further, and the process continues until the last willing buyer has acted. At that point, the marginal participant is fully invested. There is no one left to buy. The same mechanism operates in reverse during selloffs.
Distinguishing between healthy momentum and a fragile bubble is the central challenge. Momentum supported by improving fundamentals can persist for extended periods, rewarding those who ride it. Momentum that diverges from fundamentals is vulnerable. The tactical allocator must assess not only the direction of prices but the foundation on which they rest.
The pain trade crystallizes this thinking. It describes the market movement that would cause the greatest discomfort to the largest number of participants. When positioning is one-sided—when most investors are positioned for a particular outcome—the opposite movement becomes the pain trade. If most are bullish and have allocated accordingly, a decline inflicts maximum damage. If most are bearish and have hedged or sold, a rally does the same. These situations create asymmetric opportunities. The market must move only a small amount in the pain direction to force repositioning, which in turn amplifies the move.
Sentiment analysis does not provide precise timing signals. Extreme readings can persist. Fear can deepen. Greed can extend further. The tactical allocator who acts too early absorbs losses while waiting for the reversal. Combining sentiment signals with other inputs improves the odds. A valuation extreme accompanied by a sentiment extreme is more powerful than either alone—the market is both expensive and complacent, or both cheap and fearful. These conjunctions are rare, but they offer the most compelling tactical opportunities. When they appear, the tactical allocator pays attention. When they are absent, patience is the wiser course.

title: 8  Tactical Financial Analysis
section: 8.5 Technical Analysis in a Portfolio Context
text:
8.5 Technical Analysis in a Portfolio Context
Technical analysis occupies an uneasy place in the investment profession. Academics largely dismiss it. The Efficient Market Hypothesis, in its weak form, holds that past prices cannot predict future returns. Patterns in historical data should not generate excess returns. Applied managers, however, often take a different view. They use technical tools not to predict the future with certainty but to manage entry and exit points, to impose discipline on decision-making, and to assess the balance of supply and demand in markets.
The distinction matters. Technical analysis as fortune-telling is speculation. Technical analysis as a framework for risk management and execution is something else entirely. It provides a structured way to act on the signals generated by fundamental and sentiment analysis. It answers the question: we have a view, now how do we implement it?
Trend following is among the most widely used approaches. The premise is simple. Markets that have been rising tend to continue rising. Markets that have been falling tend to continue falling. Trends persist. The tactical allocator identifies the trend and positions with it, rather than against it.
Moving averages provide a systematic way to identify trends. A short-term moving average, such as the fifty-day, captures recent price action. A long-term moving average, such as the two-hundred-day, captures the broader trend. When the short-term average crosses above the long-term average, it signals that momentum is positive. This is a golden cross. When the short-term average crosses below, it signals that momentum has turned negative. This is a death cross.
These signals are not predictive in the sense of forecasting future returns. They are descriptive. They tell the tactical allocator what the market is doing, not what it will do. Their value lies in discipline. A trend-following rule forces the allocator to cut losing positions and let winning positions run. It removes the temptation to hold on to a declining asset in the hope of a recovery, or to sell a rising asset too early to lock in a small gain.
Mean reversion operates on the opposite premise. Markets that have moved too far in one direction tend to snap back. The tactical allocator identifies extremes and positions for the reversal. The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, is a common tool for this purpose. It measures the speed and magnitude of recent price changes, producing a value between zero and one hundred. Readings above seventy indicate that an asset is overbought. The buying has been too aggressive, and a pullback is likely. Readings below thirty indicate that an asset is oversold. The selling has been too aggressive, and a bounce is likely.
RSI signals are most effective in range-bound markets, where prices oscillate between established levels without a clear trend. In strongly trending markets, overbought and oversold signals can persist for extended periods. An asset in a powerful uptrend can remain overbought for weeks or months. Selling too early means missing the bulk of the move. The tactical allocator must assess the broader context before acting on a mean reversion signal.
Support and resistance levels provide a third lens. Support is a price level where buying interest has historically emerged, preventing further declines. Resistance is a price level where selling interest has historically emerged, capping further gains. These levels reflect the collective memory of the market. They are prices at which significant transactions occurred, where investors made decisions they are reluctant to reverse.
When a price approaches a support level, buyers who missed the previous opportunity may step in. When it approaches resistance, sellers who regretted not selling earlier may act. The tactical allocator uses these levels to set stop-loss orders—predetermined prices at which a position will be closed to limit further losses. If a tactical overweight to equities was based on improving economic momentum, and that momentum reverses, the position should be closed. A stop-loss placed below a key support level provides a disciplined exit, removing emotion from the decision.
Technical tools serve an integrating function. Fundamental analysis identifies the tactical opportunity. Sentiment analysis assesses whether the crowd is positioned for or against it. Technical analysis provides the framework for execution—when to enter, when to exit, and how to manage risk along the way. No single tool is sufficient. Together, they form a coherent process for tactical decision-making.
That process, however, must be followed with discipline. The tools are only as good as the hands that wield them. A trend-following signal ignored is worthless. A stop-loss that is repeatedly moved lower defeats its purpose. The behavioral pitfalls that make tactical allocation difficult—overconfidence, regret aversion, anchoring—apply as much to technical analysis as to any other approach. The tools provide structure. They do not provide immunity from human nature.

title: 8  Tactical Financial Analysis
section: 8.6 Implementing TAA: The Tracking Error Budget
text:
8.6 Implementing TAA: The Tracking Error Budget
Tactical asset allocation cannot be implemented at will. A professional firm operates within constraints, and the most important of these is the tracking error budget. This budget defines how far the actual portfolio may stray from the strategic benchmark. It is the risk control that prevents tactical enthusiasm from overwhelming the long-term plan.
Tracking error measures the volatility of the difference between the portfolio return and the benchmark return. It quantifies active risk. A tracking error of zero means the portfolio mirrors the benchmark exactly. A tracking error of 3 percent means the portfolio’s return can be expected to deviate from the benchmark by roughly 3 percent per year, in either direction. The formula is straightforward:
\[
\sigma_{\text{active}} = \sqrt{\text{Var}(R_p - R_b)}
\]
Where \(R_p\) is the portfolio return and \(R_b\) is the benchmark return. The tracking error budget sets an upper bound on this deviation. A typical mandate might allow a tracking error of 2 to 4 percent per year. Within this band, the tactical allocator can express views. Beyond it, the portfolio drifts from its strategic anchor.
The budget forces discipline. Every tactical position consumes a portion of the allowable tracking error. An overweight to equities relative to bonds consumes risk. An overweight to a specific region or sector consumes more. When the budget is exhausted, no further tactical deviations are permitted, regardless of how compelling the opportunity appears. This constraint protects the client from excessive active risk and protects the manager from the behavioral tendency to double down on losing positions.
Active share provides a related measure. Where tracking error captures the volatility of return differences, active share captures the magnitude of portfolio differences directly. It measures the percentage of the portfolio that differs from the benchmark. A portfolio with 100 percent active share holds nothing in common with the benchmark. A portfolio with 0 percent active share is the benchmark. Active share answers a different question than tracking error. Two portfolios can have the same tracking error but vastly different active shares, depending on how concentrated the active bets are.
The tactical allocator must understand both metrics. A high active share with low tracking error suggests the portfolio is making many small, uncorrelated bets. A low active share with high tracking error suggests a few concentrated, volatile bets. The optimal combination depends on the manager’s skill and the breadth of opportunities, as the Fundamental Law of Active Management implies.
Transaction costs and slippage form the third constraint. Every tactical adjustment incurs costs. Commissions are the most visible. Bid-ask spreads are less visible but often larger. A position that moves against the trader between the decision to trade and the execution suffers slippage. For large trades in less liquid markets, the market impact of the trade itself can move the price further.
These costs are the alpha-eater. A tactical signal that generates a gross excess return of 1 percent is worthless if the round-trip cost of implementing it is 1.2 percent. The net return to the client is negative. The tactical allocator must estimate costs before trading, not after. This requires an understanding of market liquidity, typical spreads, and the size of the position relative to average daily volume.
The cost constraint interacts with the tracking error budget. Higher-turnover strategies consume more costs and more of the tracking error budget. A tactical process that generates many small signals may have a higher gross information ratio but a lower net information ratio after costs. A process that generates fewer, higher-conviction signals may be cheaper to implement but harder to evaluate statistically because of the smaller sample size.
These constraints are not theoretical. They are embedded in the investment management agreement and monitored by the risk management function. The tactical allocator who ignores them will eventually breach a limit, triggering a conversation with the chief investment officer or the client. That conversation is rarely pleasant.
A disciplined implementation framework integrates the tracking error budget, active share, and cost estimates into every tactical decision. Before a trade is placed, the allocator asks three questions. How much of the tracking error budget will this consume? How does it affect the portfolio’s active share? What are the expected costs, and does the expected gross alpha exceed them by a sufficient margin? If the answers do not justify the trade, the trade is not made.
This framework keeps tactical allocation in its proper place. It is a supplement to the strategic allocation, not a replacement. It operates within defined boundaries. It must clear a cost hurdle before it is implemented. These constraints are not obstacles to performance. They are guardrails that prevent tactical enthusiasm from damaging the long-term plan.

title: 8  Tactical Financial Analysis
section: 8.7 Case Study: The Schmidt-Miller Tactical Pivot
text:
8.7 Case Study: The Schmidt-Miller Tactical Pivot
The Schmidt-Miller family’s strategic asset allocation, established in Chapter 7, positions the long-term portfolio at 35 percent global equities, 15 percent Swiss equities, 30 percent corporate bonds, and 20 percent government bonds. The equity allocation is capped at 50 percent. Portfolio volatility is held below 10 percent. These constraints reflect Klaus’s loss aversion. The allocation is designed to deliver a 6 to 8 percent return over the long term while protecting against the downside scenarios that keep Klaus awake at night.
Strategic allocations are built for normal times. They assume that the future will resemble the past, that correlations will hold, and that the economic environment will fluctuate within historical ranges. When the environment shifts, the assumptions underlying the strategic allocation come under pressure.
Consider a scenario. Global inflation, dormant for years, begins to rise. Supply chain disruptions, rising energy prices, and tight labor markets combine to push consumer prices higher. Central banks, initially slow to respond, begin to signal that rate increases are coming. The economic data weakens even as inflation remains elevated. The Investment Clock, introduced in Chapter 6, rotates from Expansion toward Stagflation.
This is the environment that most threatens the Schmidt-Miller portfolio. Stagflation punishes both equities and bonds. Equities suffer from weak growth and compressed margins. Bonds suffer from rising inflation and the rate increases that follow. The negative correlation between equities and bonds, which provides the diversification benefit at the heart of the strategic allocation, can break down. In the 1970s, both asset classes delivered negative real returns for years.
The tactical question is whether to deviate from the strategic allocation to protect against this threat. The tracking error budget allows for modest deviations. The Investment Clock signal is flashing a warning. The tactical allocator must decide whether to act.
The proposed tactical pivot is to shift 5 percent of the portfolio from long-term government bonds into gold. Government bonds are the asset class most vulnerable to rising inflation. Their fixed payments lose purchasing power as prices rise. Their duration amplifies the capital loss when yields increase. Gold, by contrast, has historically served as a store of value during inflationary periods. Its correlation with inflation expectations is positive. Its correlation with equities and bonds is low.
The trade reduces the portfolio’s exposure to the asset class most at risk and increases exposure to the asset best positioned to benefit. The cost is modest. Gold is liquid. The bid-ask spread is narrow. The 5 percent shift consumes a portion of the tracking error budget but remains well within the limits set by the IPS.
The tactical pivot alters the portfolio’s risk profile. The expected return changes little. Gold has no earnings and pays no dividends. Its long-term expected return, as estimated in Chapter 6, is roughly in line with inflation. The benefit lies not in higher expected return but in lower expected shortfall risk under the stagflation scenario. If inflation accelerates and bonds sell off, gold provides a buffer. If the stagflation threat recedes and the Investment Clock rotates back toward Recovery, the tactical position is closed. The portfolio returns to its strategic weights.
The result is evaluated against two metrics. The first is shortfall risk, introduced in Chapter 7. Does the tactical pivot reduce the probability that the portfolio fails to fund the family’s €160,000 annual withdrawal? Under the stagflation scenario, the answer is yes. The gold position cushions the portfolio against the simultaneous decline in equities and bonds. The shortfall probability, estimated through Monte Carlo simulation, declines by a measurable amount.
The second metric is tracking error. Does the tactical pivot cause the portfolio to deviate excessively from its strategic benchmark? The answer depends on the magnitude of the shift and the duration of the deviation. A 5 percent shift, held for six to twelve months, adds modest tracking error. The overall portfolio risk remains within the 10 percent volatility cap. Klaus’s binding constraint is respected.
Not all tactical pivots succeed. If the stagflation threat fails to materialize—if inflation proves transitory and growth resumes—the gold position detracts from performance. Bonds rally as rate increase expectations fade. Gold declines. The portfolio underperforms its strategic benchmark by the amount of the tactical loss, less costs.
This is the nature of tactical allocation. It is probabilistic, not certain. The tactical allocator does not need to be right every time. A process that is right more often than it is wrong, and that generates positive net returns after costs over a full cycle, adds value. The key is to keep the deviations modest, the costs low, and the evaluation horizon long enough to separate skill from noise.
For the Schmidt-Miller family, the tactical pivot serves as a form of insurance. It sacrifices a small amount of expected return in the base case to protect against a tail risk that would be particularly damaging given Klaus’s loss aversion. Whether this insurance is worth purchasing depends on the probability assigned to the stagflation scenario and the cost of the premium. The tactical allocator presents the analysis. The family decides.
This case study illustrates the proper role of tactical asset allocation within a broader wealth management framework. It is not a separate activity, disconnected from the strategic plan. It is a disciplined response to changing conditions, operating within defined boundaries, evaluated against clear metrics, and ultimately serving the same goals that the strategic allocation was designed to achieve. Tactical allocation does not replace the strategic allocation. It protects it.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.1 Introduction
Chapter 8 established the theoretical foundation for tactical decision-making. We examined the economic signals, sentiment indicators, and technical tools that inform short-term deviations from the strategic allocation. We also examined the constraints—the tracking error budget, the cost hurdle, and the behavioral pitfalls—that keep tactical allocation in its proper place. This chapter turns from theory to practice. It addresses the mechanics of implementing tactical views within a portfolio that remains anchored to its long-term policy weights.
Tactical asset allocation is not a separate portfolio. It is a tilt applied to the existing strategic allocation. The strategic weights remain the baseline. The tactical views are expressed as deviations from those weights. An overweight to equities does not mean abandoning the strategic allocation. It means holding more equities and less of something else for a defined period, until the tactical signal fades or the strategic weights are restored.
This framing matters. It keeps tactical allocation in perspective. The strategic allocation does the bulk of the work. It provides the beta that drives long-term returns. Tactical tilts provide marginal adjustments, seeking alpha at the edges. A portfolio that is 50 percent equities and 50 percent bonds under the strategic allocation might become 55 percent equities and 45 percent bonds under a tactical overweight. The shift is meaningful but not transformative. The portfolio remains recognizable.
The active weight captures this relationship. It is the difference between the actual portfolio weight and the strategic benchmark weight for each asset class.
\[
w_{a,i} = w_{p,i} - w_{b,i}
\]
Where \(w_{a,i}\) is the active weight of asset class \(i\), \(w_{p,i}\) is its actual weight in the portfolio, and \(w_{b,i}\) is its weight in the strategic benchmark. An active weight of zero means the portfolio matches the benchmark. A positive active weight means the asset is overweight. A negative active weight means it is underweight. The sum of active weights across all asset classes is zero. Every overweight must be funded by an underweight elsewhere.
This funding requirement imposes a discipline that derivatives-based approaches can circumvent. When tactical views are expressed through futures or swaps, an overweight can be added without selling anything. The leverage embedded in the derivative provides the funding. But for many private clients, including the Schmidt-Miller family, derivatives are either prohibited or viewed with suspicion. The tactical allocation must be implemented through physical securities. Selling is required to buy. The decision to overweight one asset is simultaneously a decision to underweight another.
The funding requirement forces clarity. The tactical allocator cannot simply express enthusiasm for an asset class. The enthusiasm must be paired with a corresponding lack of enthusiasm for something else. If equities are overvalued and bonds are even more overvalued, an underweight to equities requires an overweight to bonds—a choice that may be uncomfortable. If both are unattractive, the tactical allocator may choose to remain at strategic weights. Doing nothing is a valid tactical decision.
This chapter develops the mechanics of tactical implementation. We examine how active weights are constructed, how the funding decision shapes the overall risk profile, and how tactical tilts interact with the rebalancing policy that maintains the strategic allocation. We also address the practical challenges of implementing tactical views in a multi-asset, multi-currency portfolio. The goal is not to prescribe a single approach but to provide a framework within which disciplined tactical decisions can be made.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.2 Tactical Constraints
Tactical asset allocation operates within boundaries. The strategic allocation anchors the portfolio, and tactical tilts are deviations from that anchor. Without constraints, tactical enthusiasm overwhelms the long-term plan. The portfolio drifts. Risk increases. The client’s objectives, carefully documented in the IPS, are no longer served.
Tactical corridors are the primary constraint. They define the allowable range around each strategic weight. If the strategic allocation to equities is 40 percent, a tactical corridor of plus or minus 5 percentage points means the actual equity weight can range from 35 to 45 percent. Within that band, the tactical allocator expresses views. Beyond it, no further deviation is permitted.
Corridors serve multiple purposes simultaneously. They limit active risk by capping the size of any single tilt, preventing the portfolio from becoming excessively concentrated in an asset class that has performed well. They provide a mechanism for disciplined rebalancing: when an asset class breaches its corridor, it is trimmed back to within the allowable range, locking in gains and returning the portfolio to its intended risk profile. The width of the corridor depends on the asset class. More volatile assets typically warrant wider bands because their weights fluctuate more even without tactical intervention. A 5 percent corridor for equities, with volatility of 16 percent, will be breached more frequently than the same corridor for government bonds, with volatility of 6 percent. Corridor width also reflects conviction. A tactical process with a high Information Coefficient can justify greater latitude because the skill of the allocator warrants more room to act.
Active risk provides a complementary constraint. Where corridors limit the size of individual tilts, tracking error limits the risk of the active portfolio as a whole. The formula uses the covariance matrix developed in Chapter 6:
\[
\sigma_{\text{active}} = \sqrt{w_a^T \Sigma w_a}
\]
Where \(w_a\) is the vector of active weights and \(\Sigma\) is the covariance matrix of asset class returns. This single number captures the total active risk embedded in the portfolio, accounting for the correlations among the active bets. Two tilts that are individually within their corridors might combine to produce excessive tracking error if they are highly correlated. The ex-ante tracking error catches this interaction.
A typical mandate limits ex-ante tracking error to 2 or 3 percent per year. This constraint sits above the individual corridors. Even if every active weight is within its allowable range, the total active risk cannot exceed the tracking error budget. If a proposed tilt would push the ex-ante tracking error above the limit, it must be scaled back or abandoned. The two constraints work together: corridors provide simple, transparent limits that are easy to communicate, while tracking error provides a more sophisticated measure that accounts for the covariance structure of the portfolio.
These constraints also protect the tactical allocator from behavioral errors. Loss aversion, overconfidence, and anchoring bias—well documented in Chapter 4—can lead a manager to increase tactical positions after a loss, hoping to recover, or after a win, convinced of infallibility. Corridors and tracking error limits act as guardrails when judgment falters.
For a portfolio that does not use derivatives, these constraints are the primary risk management tool. There is no quick hedge to offset a tactical position that has gone wrong. The only way to reduce risk is to sell the position and return to strategic weights. The corridor sets the boundary at which that exit becomes mandatory. The tactical allocator can exit earlier, but the corridor ensures that exit cannot come later.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.3 Physical Rebalancing
Tactical decisions are made in the abstract. They are executed in the market. The difference between the two is friction, and friction costs money.
When a tactical allocator decides to shift 5 percent of the portfolio from bonds to equities, that decision is recorded at a decision price—the price prevailing when the order is conceived. The trade, however, executes at a different price, often worse. Between decision and execution, the market moves. The order itself may move the market further. Commissions are paid. Spreads are crossed. The realized outcome falls short of the initial expectation. Implementation shortfall measures this gap. It is the total cost of translating a decision into a position, and it can be broken into components.
Commissions are the most visible element—the explicit fee paid to the broker for executing the trade. For institutional investors, these are small, measured in basis points. For private clients trading through less efficient channels, they can be larger. Bid-ask spreads are less visible but often more significant. The spread is the difference between the price at which a market maker will buy and the price at which they will sell. Crossing the spread is a cost. For liquid assets like large-cap equities, the spread is narrow. For less liquid assets—certain corporate bonds, smaller market equities—it can be substantial.
Market impact is the third component and the hardest to measure. A large order moves the market against the trader. Buying pushes the price up. Selling pushes it down. The larger the order relative to typical trading volume, the greater the impact. A tactical shift of 5 percent of an €18 million portfolio is an order of €900,000. In a liquid market, that order might execute without significant impact. In a smaller market, the impact can be material.
These costs must be estimated before the trade. The tactical signal that generates a gross expected return of 1 percent is worthless if the round-trip cost of implementing it is 1.2 percent. The net return is negative. The alpha has been eaten.
Cash drag introduces a further complication. When a tactical shift requires selling one asset to buy another, there is typically a gap between the sale and the purchase. Settlement periods differ across markets. Equities settle in two days. Bonds may settle on different timelines. Currencies add another layer. During this gap, the proceeds sit in cash, earning little to nothing. If equities rally while the portfolio waits for bond proceeds to settle, the tactical gain evaporates. Managing this requires operational attention. Trades should be coordinated so that settlement dates align. Where a gap is unavoidable, the expected market movement during that gap should be incorporated into the cost estimate.
The tactical allocator who ignores implementation shortfall is flying blind. The allocator who measures it, estimates it in advance, and structures trades to minimize it has an edge. That edge is not alpha in the traditional sense—it is not a forecast of market direction. But costs avoided are returns earned. In a zero-sum game where gross alpha is scarce, operational discipline can make the difference between a tactical process that adds value and one that does not.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.4 The Brinson-Fachler Model
A tactical process makes promises. It promises that deviations from the strategic allocation will add value, that the tilts will be right more often than wrong, and that the net result after costs will be positive. Performance attribution tests these promises. It decomposes the portfolio’s return into components that reveal exactly where value was added and where it was destroyed.
The Brinson-Fachler model provides the framework. It separates the total active return—the difference between the portfolio return and the benchmark return—into two primary effects: the allocation effect and the selection effect. The allocation effect measures whether the tactical tilts were in the right direction. The selection effect measures whether the specific securities or funds chosen within each asset class outperformed the class benchmark.
The allocation effect answers a simple question. Did we overweight the asset classes that performed well and underweight those that performed poorly? It is calculated as:
\[
\text{Allocation Effect} = (w_{p,i} - w_{b,i}) \times (R_{b,i} - R_{b,\text{total}})
\]
Where \(w_{p,i}\) is the portfolio weight in asset class \(i\), \(w_{b,i}\) is the benchmark weight, \(R_{b,i}\) is the benchmark return for that asset class, and \(R_{b,\text{total}}\) is the total benchmark return. The term \((R_{b,i} - R_{b,\text{total}})\) captures whether the asset class outperformed or underperformed the overall benchmark. A positive allocation effect means the tactical overweights were in asset classes that beat the benchmark and the underweights were in asset classes that lagged.
The selection effect answers a different question. Within each asset class, did the specific investments chosen outperform the asset class benchmark? It is calculated as:
\[
\text{Selection Effect} = w_{b,i} \times (R_{p,i} - R_{b,i})
\]
Where \(R_{p,i}\) is the actual return earned on the portfolio’s holdings in asset class \(i\). A positive selection effect means the chosen securities or active managers beat the passive benchmark for that class.
These two effects are distinct. A tactical allocator can be right about the direction of an asset class but wrong about the specific implementation—a good allocation decision undermined by poor security selection. Conversely, excellent security selection within an asset class can be swamped by a poor allocation decision that underweighted the very class in which the selection skill was demonstrated.
The interaction effect captures the overlap between the two. It accounts for the fact that an overweight to an asset class in which security selection also added value produces a combined benefit greater than the sum of the separate effects. In the Brinson-Fachler framework, the interaction effect is:
\[
\text{Interaction Effect} = (w_{p,i} - w_{b,i}) \times (R_{p,i} - R_{b,i})
\]
The total active return is the sum of all three effects across all asset classes. If the tactical process added value, the total active return is positive. If it destroyed value, the total is negative.
For the Schmidt-Miller family, this attribution provides accountability. Klaus, analytical by nature, will want to see the breakdown. He will ask whether the tactical tilts worked. The Brinson-Fachler table provides the answer. It shows, in currency terms, the contribution of each decision.
Consider a simplified example. The portfolio held an overweight to global equities of 5 percent relative to the strategic benchmark. Global equities returned 8 percent over the period, while the total benchmark returned 5 percent. The allocation effect for this decision is positive: 0.05 multiplied by 3 percent, or 15 basis points of value added. If, within the equity allocation, the chosen fund returned 7.5 percent against a benchmark of 8 percent, the selection effect is negative: the benchmark weight multiplied by negative 50 basis points. The interaction effect captures the combination.
The Brinson-Fachler model serves multiple audiences. For the client, it provides transparency. For the investment committee, it provides accountability. For the tactical allocator, it provides a diagnostic tool. A consistently negative allocation effect suggests the tactical signals are flawed. A consistently negative selection effect suggests the implementation is poor. The attribution points to where the problem lies.
Measurement without action is sterile. The tactical allocator uses the attribution results to refine the process. If the allocation effect is persistently negative, the signals require review. Perhaps the valuation metrics are mistimed. Perhaps the sentiment indicators are giving false readings. If the selection effect is negative, the choice of funds or securities within each asset class needs attention. The Brinson-Fachler framework not only answers the question of whether value was added. It shows where to look when value is not being added.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.5 The Black-Litterman Active Tilt
Chapter 7 introduced the Black-Litterman model as a framework for strategic asset allocation. The same framework extends naturally to tactical tilts. Where strategic Black-Litterman starts from market equilibrium weights and tilts toward long-term views, tactical Black-Litterman starts from the strategic allocation and tilts toward short-term views. The mechanism is the same. Only the reference portfolio and the horizon of the views differ.
The tactical version of the model answers a practical question. Given a view on an asset class, expressed with a specific degree of confidence, how many euros should move from one bucket to another? The answer depends on three factors: the strength of the view, the confidence in that view, and the risk characteristics of the assets involved.
A strong view warrants a larger tilt. If the tactical allocator believes that global equities will outperform bonds by 3 percent over the next quarter, the active weight should be larger than if the expected outperformance is only 1 percent. This relationship is captured by the view vector \(Q\) in the Black-Litterman formula. A larger value in \(Q\) translates, all else equal, to a larger active weight.
Confidence modulates the tilt. A view held with high conviction—reflected in a small value of \(\omega\) in the diagonal matrix \(\Omega\)—produces a larger deviation from the strategic weights. A view held with low conviction produces a smaller deviation. This is the mechanism that prevents the tactical allocator from overreacting to weak signals. If the evidence is ambiguous, the model stays close to the strategic allocation. If the evidence is compelling, the model tilts further.
The risk characteristics of the assets involved also shape the tilt. An overweight to equities funded by an underweight to government bonds is a high-risk active bet because the two asset classes have low correlation. The tracking error consumed by this tilt is substantial. An overweight to equities funded by corporate bonds is a lower-risk bet because the correlations are higher. The Black-Litterman framework incorporates these relationships through the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). The same view expressed through different funding pairs produces different active weights.
The practical benefit is that Black-Litterman scales the deviation automatically. The tactical allocator does not need to guess at the appropriate active weight. The model calculates it based on the stated view, the stated confidence, and the covariance structure of the portfolio. A low-confidence view on Swiss equities might result in a tilt of only 1 or 2 percent, an amount so small that it barely registers against the strategic allocation. This is by design. The model recognizes that acting on weak views generates unnecessary trading costs without a commensurate increase in expected return.
The cost-awareness of the model is one of its strengths. Every tactical trade incurs the frictions described in Section 9.3: commissions, spreads, market impact, and cash drag. A tilt that is too small to overcome these costs should not be implemented. The Black-Litterman framework, by scaling the active weight to the confidence in the view, naturally suppresses small trades. Only views that are strong enough to generate a meaningful active weight survive the implicit cost filter.
For the Schmidt-Miller portfolio, tactical Black-Litterman operates within the corridors established in Section 9.2. The active weights produced by the model are checked against the allowable ranges. If a calculated tilt exceeds the corridor, it is capped at the corridor limit. The tracking error budget provides a second check. If the collection of tactical tilts exceeds the ex-ante tracking error limit, the tilts are scaled back proportionally.
The process integrates conviction, risk, and cost into a single framework. The tactical allocator specifies the view and the confidence. The model calculates the trade. The constraints ensure that the trade remains within the bounds set by the IPS and the tracking error budget. What emerges is a disciplined approach to tactical allocation, one that respects both the opportunities that markets present and the frictions that real-world implementation imposes.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.6 The Friction of Physical Trading
Tactical asset allocation assumes that assets can be traded freely, that the only frictions are commissions and spreads. For taxable investors, this assumption breaks down. Every sale crystallizes a gain or a loss. Every gain triggers a tax liability. The tax cost of a tactical trade can exceed all other costs combined.
For the Schmidt-Miller family, this is not an abstract concern. Elke’s inherited portfolio carries a low cost basis. Selling any portion of it triggers a 20 percent capital gains tax on the appreciation. A tactical shift that requires selling €100,000 of inherited Swiss equities, with a cost basis of €20,000, generates a tax bill of €16,000. The tactical signal must generate enough excess return to cover that bill and still leave something for the client. The hurdle is high.
The after-tax hurdle rate formalizes this requirement. A tactical trade that generates a gross excess return of 2 percent is not attractive if the tax cost of implementing it consumes 1.5 percent. The net after-tax return is a mere 0.5 percent. When that thin margin is further reduced by commissions, spreads, and potential cash drag, it can vanish entirely. The tactical allocator must evaluate every trade on an after-tax basis. The question is not “does this trade add value?” but “does this trade add value after the tax bill is paid?”
This reality shifts the calculus of tactical allocation. Trades that look attractive in a tax-exempt account become marginal or negative in a taxable one. The tactical process must clear a higher bar. Only signals that are both strong and timely justify the tax cost of implementation.
Strategic tax-loss harvesting offers a partial solution. When the portfolio holds positions with unrealized losses, those losses can be realized to offset gains elsewhere. The proceeds from selling a losing position fund the purchase of the tactical overweight without triggering a net tax liability. The loss harvest neutralizes the tax impact.
Timing matters. Losses are most abundant during market downturns, exactly when tactical signals may indicate that risk assets are attractive. A portfolio battered by a market decline may hold numerous positions with unrealized losses. The tactical allocator can sell some of those positions, book the losses for tax purposes, and reinvest the proceeds in the assets that the tactical signal favors. The trade cleans up the portfolio while positioning for the recovery.
This approach requires coordination between the tactical process and the tax management function. Not every losing position should be sold. The asset sold should be one that the portfolio can afford to lose, that aligns with the tactical underweight, and that generates a loss large enough to offset the gain from the tactical sale. The replacement asset should maintain the portfolio’s strategic exposure while capturing the tactical opportunity.
The constraint is real, but it is not paralyzing. A taxable portfolio can still engage in tactical allocation. It simply must do so with greater care. Trades must be larger and more conviction-driven to overcome the tax hurdle. Holding periods must be longer to amortize the tax cost over more expected return. And the tactical process must integrate tax awareness into every decision, not as an afterthought but as a core component of the implementation framework. The tax tail does not wag the investment dog, but it certainly shapes how the dog moves.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.7 Behavioral Pitfalls in Execution
Tactical allocation demands discipline. The frameworks are elegant. The models are precise. But the person executing the trades is human, subject to the same biases that distort all decision-making under uncertainty. Three pitfalls deserve particular attention.
Portfolio churn is the urge to tinker. Markets are noisy. Prices move daily. News flows ceaselessly. The temptation to respond—to adjust, to tweak, to do something—is constant. Each trade feels proactive, a demonstration of engagement and expertise. Yet the costs accumulate with every transaction. Commissions, spreads, and taxes chip away at returns, while the benefits of each individual trade remain uncertain. The tactical allocator must distinguish between signals that warrant action and noise that should be ignored. Most market movements are noise. The default posture should be patience.
Status quo bias pulls in the opposite direction. It is the reluctance to act even when action is warranted. Selling a position that has performed well feels wrong. The winner has delivered returns. It has proven itself. Why abandon it? Buying a position that has performed poorly feels equally wrong. The loser has destroyed value. It carries the stigma of failure. Yet tactical allocation often requires exactly these uncomfortable moves: selling strength and buying weakness. The signals discussed in Chapter 8—valuation spreads, sentiment extremes, mean reversion—point toward assets that are out of favor and away from those that are loved. Acting on these signals means overriding the emotional attachment to what has worked and the aversion to what has not.
The tension between churn and inertia is resolved by process. A documented framework specifies when to act and when to stand still. Tactical corridors define the boundaries. The cost hurdle filters out marginal trades. The tracking error budget enforces restraint. When a signal breaches the threshold, the trade is executed without further debate. When no signal breaches, the portfolio remains untouched. The process, not the emotion of the moment, governs the decision.
Window dressing is a different kind of failure. It occurs when trades are motivated not by investment considerations but by appearance. A position that has declined is sold before a client meeting so it does not appear on the quarterly statement. A fashionable asset is purchased to demonstrate awareness of the latest trend. The trades are not grounded in tactical signals. They are cosmetic, designed to manage perception rather than portfolio risk.
The antidote is transparency. Every trade should be linked to a documented rationale. The Brinson-Fachler attribution framework, introduced in Section 9.4, exposes cosmetic trades for what they are: deviations without purpose, costs without benefit. A quarterly review that traces each tactical decision back to its original signal and evaluates its contribution to performance leaves no room for window dressing.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
text:
9.8 Case Study: Schmidt-Miller Tactical Audit
The Schmidt-Miller portfolio held 12 percent in global government bonds as part of its strategic allocation. In early 2024, inflation data began to surprise to the upside. Energy prices rose. Wage growth accelerated. The Investment Clock rotated toward Stagflation. The tactical signal, based on the macro-fundamental analysis from Section 8.3, indicated an overweight to commodities and an underweight to long-term government bonds.
The tactical allocator proposed a shift of €500,000, roughly 2.5 percent of the long-term portfolio, from global government bonds into a diversified commodity ETF. The trade was within the tactical corridors. The tracking error budget could absorb it. The thesis was that inflation would continue to surprise and that commodities would outperform bonds over the next two quarters.
The trade worked. Commodities returned 9 percent over the holding period. Government bonds returned 2 percent. The gross excess return on the tactical position was 7 percent, or €35,000. Applying the Brinson-Fachler framework, the allocation effect was positive. The decision to overweight commodities and underweight bonds added approximately 40 basis points to the overall portfolio return. On paper, a success.
Then the costs were subtracted.
The commodity ETF carried an expense ratio of 0.35 percent. The bid-ask spread on the ETF was 0.15 percent. The bond sale triggered a realized capital gain of €20,000, on which a 20 percent tax was owed—a liability of €4,000. Commissions on both trades totaled €500. Cash drag during the two-day settlement gap, when markets moved favorably, cost an estimated €300. The total cost of implementation was approximately €5,200.
The net gain after all costs was €29,800. The net excess return was roughly 6 percent, or 35 basis points of portfolio-level contribution. The tactical trade added value, but less than the gross numbers suggested. The frictions of physical trading consumed nearly 15 percent of the gross alpha.
This is the reality of tactical allocation for a taxable investor. The trade was well-conceived, properly sized, and successfully timed. It cleared the cost hurdle. But the margin of success was narrower than a naive analysis would indicate. The next trade, equally sound in conception, might fail to clear the hurdle if the signal is weaker or the costs are higher.
The audit reinforces the discipline. Every tactical decision carries a tax consequence. Every trade consumes a portion of the tracking error budget. Implementation shortfall is not a theoretical concept. It is measured in euros, and it compounds. The tactical allocator who internalizes these frictions—who treats the after-tax, after-cost return as the only return that matters—will trade less often, with greater conviction, and with a clearer understanding of what it takes to add value in the real world.

title: 9  Tactical Asset Allocation
section: 9.9 Tactical Asset Allocation in the IMAG Simulation
text:
9.9 Tactical Asset Allocation in the IMAG Simulation
The framework developed in this chapter is applied directly in the IMAG simulation. We have established the strategic allocation as our benchmark. The task now is to determine whether and how to deviate from it. Tactical allocation in the simulation is the deliberate, short-term tilt away from the strategic weights, based on our reading of current market conditions. The strategic allocation anchors the portfolio. Tactical tilts express our views about which market segments will outperform in the near term.

9.9.1 From Strategic Benchmark to Tactical Tilts
The simulation separates strategic and tactical allocation explicitly. The strategic allocation, set on the Clients tab, serves as the benchmark. The tactical allocation, set on the same page after disabling the automatic tactical allocation, allows us to adjust weights in response to the Economic Outlook. By default, the simulation copies the strategic allocation into the tactical allocation. If we hold no views about near-term market direction, we remain at the strategic benchmark. This is consistent with the Black-Litterman logic we examined: start from the equilibrium portfolio and deviate only where the data provides a genuine insight.






Figure 9.1: Tactical Allocation Decision



The tracking error that results from our tactical deviations is estimated and displayed. The projected information ratio, calculated automatically based on forecasted returns and the estimated tracking error, tells us whether our tilts are expected to add value relative to the risk we are taking. This is the Fundamental Law of Active Management in practice. The information ratio depends on the skill of our forecasts and the breadth of our bets. If we tilt aggressively based on weak signals, the tracking error rises without a commensurate increase in expected return, and the information ratio falls.
The disciplines we established in this chapter apply directly. Tactical deviations should be modest. The strategic allocation does the heavy lifting. Our tilts should be grounded in a clear thesis derived from the Economic Outlook. If the data shows the US economy in recovery with rising confidence and falling unemployment, we might overweight US equities and underweight US government bonds. If Europe remains in an accommodative policy environment with low inflation and continued quantitative easing, we might overweight European equities relative to European bonds. Each tilt is a view, and each view consumes a portion of the tracking error budget.
The tactical corridors we discussed provide the boundaries. The simulation does not impose explicit corridor limits, but the discipline must come from us. An overweight of 5 percent to an equity segment is a meaningful tilt. An overweight of 20 percent is a bet that the strategic allocation was wrong. The latter may occasionally be justified, but it carries a burden of proof that should give any disciplined allocator pause.


9.9.2 From Tactical Allocation to Asset-Level Positions
When the automatic asset-level allocation is enabled, the simulation translates our tactical weights into specific positions within each market segment. Equities are distributed according to market value weights by default. Other segments use equal weighting. This automation reflects the principle that tactical allocation is about asset class and currency decisions, not individual security selection. We are expressing views about market segments, not about specific companies.






Figure 9.2: Markets Page



When we disable the automatic asset-level allocation, we take direct control of individual positions on the Markets page. This page lists all investable assets with data on performance, benchmark weight, and factor loadings. We can sort and filter by asset class, currency, and industry. Clicking on an asset reveals instrument details including historical prices, performance metrics, and fundamental data. This granularity allows us to implement our tactical views with precision. If we hold a view that value stocks will outperform, we can tilt the equity allocation toward assets with high value factor loadings. If we believe a specific sector will benefit from current economic conditions, we can overweight that sector within the equity segment.
The cost of this granularity is the risk of overconfidence. The more decisions we make at the asset level, the more opportunities we have to be wrong. The Fundamental Law reminds us that breadth helps only if we have genuine skill. If our stock-level forecasts have no predictive power, adding more bets simply increases noise and trading costs. The automation exists for a reason. It allows us to focus our attention where we are most likely to add value: the tactical tilts between asset classes and currencies, grounded in the macroeconomic analysis from the Economic Outlook.


9.9.3 Evaluating Tactical Performance
The Analyst page provides the tools for performance attribution. After each round, we can decompose our returns to understand which tactical decisions contributed and which detracted. This is the Brinson-Fachler framework in practice. The attribution analysis covers currency, asset class, industry, maturity, and factor exposures. It answers the questions we posed in this chapter. Did our tactical tilts add value? Was the allocation effect positive, meaning we overweighted the segments that outperformed? Was the selection effect positive, meaning our specific asset choices within each segment beat their benchmarks?






Figure 9.3: Analyst Page



The strategic allocation analysis on the same page assesses how well our portfolio meets the needs of each client type. This compares our decisions to the optimal allocation embedded in the game’s parameters. It closes the loop between client analysis and portfolio construction. If our strategic allocation was set correctly, reflecting the client’s risk tolerance and return objectives, this analysis will confirm alignment. If we misjudged the client, the gap will be visible here.
The Analyst page also provides visibility into the fund management team. Higher salaries attract more skilled analysts, and more skilled analysts provide more accurate forecasts. This mirrors the real-world trade-off we discussed. Research costs money. Better research costs more. The tactical allocator must decide whether the improved signal quality justifies the expense. If higher analyst salaries produce an IC of 0.12 instead of 0.08, the Fundamental Law tells us the information ratio improves. Whether that improvement covers the salary cost is the calculation every fund manager must make.


9.9.4 The Friction of Implementation
The costs we examined in this chapter are present in the simulation, though some are more visible than others. Trading costs, while not itemized on every trade, are embedded in the market dynamics. Frequent tactical adjustments generate more costs than patient, conviction-driven tilts. The tax consequences of realizing gains, so critical for the Schmidt-Miller family’s inherited portfolio, are modeled in the simulation’s treatment of portfolio returns.
The discipline the simulation rewards is the same discipline the chapter advocates. Trade with conviction, not out of boredom. Anchor every tactical decision in a specific, testable thesis derived from the economic data. Evaluate performance honestly, using the attribution tools to separate skill from luck. Respect the tracking error budget, knowing that each tilt consumes risk capacity that cannot be recovered. When the data provides no clear signal, remain at the strategic benchmark. Doing nothing is a valid tactical decision.
The simulation’s automation tools support this discipline. By default, tactical weights equal strategic weights. We must actively choose to deviate, which imposes a moment of reflection. The attribution analysis forces us to confront the results of our decisions. The strategic allocation analysis reminds us that the ultimate measure of success is not whether we beat a benchmark but whether we meet the client’s needs. These features do not guarantee good decisions, but they create an environment in which disciplined tactical allocation can be practiced and evaluated.

title: 10  Security Analysis
text:
10.1 Introduction
The preceding chapters moved from the client’s circumstances to the strategic asset allocation. We established the policy mix. We examined tactical tilts. We addressed the constraints of implementation. What remains is the final step: selecting the specific securities that will populate each asset class allocation.
Security analysis is the process of evaluating individual investments for their suitability. It asks not whether equities as a class are attractive, but whether a particular stock, bond, or fund merits the capital it would receive. The strategic allocation provides the architecture. Security analysis provides the materials. A sound allocation can be undermined by poor security selection, just as a well-designed building can be compromised by faulty materials.
This distinction connects directly to the Brinson-Fachler attribution framework from Chapter 9. Recall that the model decomposes active return into allocation effects and selection effects. The allocation effect captures whether overweighting or underweighting an asset class added value. The selection effect captures whether the specific securities chosen within that asset class beat its benchmark. Security analysis feeds the selection effect. It is the engine that drives the \(R_{p,i} - R_{b,i}\) term in the Brinson-Fachler formula. A positive selection effect means the securities chosen outperformed the asset class benchmark. Security analysis is the discipline that seeks to make that happen.
At its core, security analysis rests on a simple distinction: intrinsic value versus market price. Intrinsic value is what an asset is worth, based on its expected future cash flows, its risk, and its growth prospects. Market price is what the market is willing to pay for it today. The two are not always equal. Markets are mostly efficient, as Chapter 8 discussed, but they are not perfectly efficient. Sentiment, liquidity, and institutional constraints can push prices away from intrinsic value. Security analysis seeks to identify those gaps, to buy assets trading below their intrinsic value and to avoid or sell those trading above it.
The approach taken depends on the asset class. For equities, fundamental analysis examines financial statements, competitive position, and management quality. For bonds, credit analysis assesses the issuer’s ability to meet its obligations. For funds and ETFs, the analysis shifts to the manager’s process, the fee structure, and the tracking error relative to the benchmark. Each asset class requires its own analytical framework, but the underlying question is the same: is this security priced in a way that compensates us adequately for the risks we are taking?
This chapter surveys the methods of security analysis. We begin with the macroeconomic context, then examine fundamental equity analysis, fixed income analysis, and quantitative screening approaches. The treatment is not exhaustive—entire textbooks are devoted to each method—but it provides the framework within which security selection decisions are made. The chapter concludes by populating the Schmidt-Miller portfolio with specific securities, translating the strategic weights from Chapter 7 into a concrete set of holdings.

title: 10  Security Analysis
section: 10.2 Fundamental Equity Analysis: The Bottom-Up Approach
text:
10.2 Fundamental Equity Analysis: The Bottom-Up Approach
Fundamental equity analysis seeks to determine the intrinsic value of a company by examining its financial statements, its competitive position, and its prospects for future growth. It is a bottom-up approach. It begins with the company itself, not with the economy or the sector, though both provide context for the assessment.
Financial statement analysis forms the foundation. The three primary statements—the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement—tell the story of a business in numbers. Revenue growth reveals whether the company is expanding or stagnating. Profit margins reveal its pricing power and cost discipline. Return on equity reveals how efficiently it deploys shareholder capital. But the raw numbers are only a starting point. The analyst must assess their quality.
Quality of earnings refers to the sustainability and reliability of reported profits. A company that consistently meets or beats earnings estimates may be managing earnings through aggressive revenue recognition, changes in inventory accounting, or the timing of expenses. Cash flow conversion provides a check. If reported earnings are strong but operating cash flow is weak, the earnings may be of low quality. The cash flow statement strips away non-cash items and reveals how much actual cash the business generates. A high ratio of operating cash flow to net income suggests that earnings are backed by real cash. A low ratio suggests the opposite.
Capital structure analysis examines how the company finances its operations. The mix of debt and equity affects both risk and return. High leverage amplifies returns when business conditions are favorable but increases the risk of financial distress when they deteriorate.
